title: Arrow Functions
summary: An arrow function is a shorter way to write many JavaScript functions.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: `const double = n => n * 2` creates a function whose result is the expression after the arrow. It is like a tiny recipe: give it a number and it returns twice that amount. Parentheses make the parameter explicit when needed, and braces are useful when multiple statements are required. For example, use an arrow in map when each item should become a display label.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: Use parentheses around multiple parameters, such as `(price, tax) => price + tax`. The parameters are the inputs the function receives. It is like listing each ingredient before the recipe begins. With zero parameters, write `() => value` so JavaScript can tell the function has no inputs. For example, wrap two inputs in parentheses so the function signature is clear.

subtopics.title: Common choice
subtopics.explanation: Use braces for a function body with several statements. Add `return` when the function should send a value back. It is like opening a longer instruction card with several steps. Without an explicit return, a brace-bodied arrow function returns `undefined`. For example, add braces and return when a calculation needs validation before its result.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: A callback is a function passed to another operation so it can be called later. Array methods, event listeners, and timers often use callbacks. It is like handing a helper a task to perform at the right moment. Keep callbacks small and name them when the behavior deserves a clear label. For example, name a callback when inline logic becomes difficult to understand.

subtopics.title: Use it safely
subtopics.explanation: An arrow function does not create its own `this`; it uses the surrounding value. This differs from a regular function, where `this` depends on how it is called. It is like borrowing the current room’s address instead of receiving a new one. Use regular functions when a method needs its own call-bound `this`. For example, use a regular method when its own call-bound this value is required.

foundations.overview: An arrow function is a shorter way to write a JavaScript function. It is common for small callbacks, such as transforming each item in a list. Think of it like a compact instruction card passed to another operation. Arrow functions also treat `this` differently from regular functions, so choose them because their behavior fits the situation, not only because they use fewer characters.
foundations.whyItMatters: Arrow functions are common in callbacks, but syntax choice affects this and return behavior. Knowing those rules avoids subtle bugs while keeping small transformations concise.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine creates no `this`/`arguments` slot for an arrow's execution context, so referencing them resolves up the scope chain — exactly like any other free variable. This is why call/apply/bind cannot influence an arrow's `this`.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Array transformations, promise `.then` callbacks, setTimeout/setInterval callbacks, React inline handlers, and small pure helpers are almost always written as arrow functions.
foundations.businessImpact: Concise callbacks improve readability and reduce boilerplate, which speeds feature delivery; correct lexical `this` avoids handler crashes that would otherwise hurt the user experience.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Arrows reduce the need for `that = this` workarounds and `.bind(this)` calls, making asynchronous and event code cleaner and less error-prone.
foundations.performanceImpact: Arrows are as fast as regular functions to call; the main consideration is that inline arrows in render paths create a new function each render, which can defeat memoization — define them once when identity matters.
commonUseCases: Short callbacks for map, filter, reduce, and forEach
Preserving the surrounding this inside object/class methods
Small pure helper functions and one-liners

commonMisconceptions.myth: Arrow functions are just shorter regular functions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They behave differently: no own this/arguments, cannot be new'd, and no prototype — so they are not always interchangeable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should use arrow functions for object methods to keep `this` pointing at the object.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It does the opposite — an arrow method captures the OUTER this (often window/undefined), so the object's own methods should be regular functions.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An arrow is interchangeable with every regular function.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Arrow functions inherit this and differ in constructor and arguments behavior.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A shorter callback is always more readable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Name or expand complex logic when a compact expression hides the steps.

visualExplorer.caption: See how a regular callback collapses into a concise arrow function, step by step.

config.intro: Start from a verbose function expression and progressively apply each arrow shorthand rule.

steps.name: Start verbose
steps.detail: function (n) { return n * 2; } — full syntax with keyword, braces, and return.

steps.name: Drop `function`, add =>
steps.detail: (n) => { return n * 2; } — same behavior, arrow syntax.

steps.name: Single param: drop parens
steps.detail: n => { return n * 2; } — one parameter needs no parentheses.

steps.name: Single expression: implicit return
steps.detail: n => n * 2 — drop braces and `return`; the expression's value is returned.

steps.name: Returning an object
steps.detail: n => ({ value: n }) — wrap object literals in parens so they aren't read as a block.

interactiveExamples.title: Concise syntax and implicit return
interactiveExamples.explanation: The arrow versions are shorter and return automatically. Returning an object literal needs parentheses.

interactiveExamples.title: Lexical this saves a callback
interactiveExamples.explanation: Inside the method, the arrow keeps `this` as the timer object, so it can read this.label. A regular function callback would lose it.

hints: A single parameter does not need parentheses.
A single-expression body needs no braces or return keyword.
